intro: From 56kbps dial-up to fiber-to-the-home — how Pakistan's physical internet backbone was built, and why it still occasionally falls over.

facts.heading: Dial-Up Beginnings (1992–1998)
facts.detail: Imran-Net launched Pakistan's first commercial dial-up service in 1992-93, alongside the UNDP-funded SDNPK project offering early email and newsgroup access. By 1998, speeds reached 56kbps and internet calls were exempted from multi-metering charges.
facts.source: Ispak — History of Internet in Pakistan

facts.heading: Pakistan's First Submarine Cable (2000)
facts.detail: PTCL brought the SEA-ME-WE-3 submarine cable system into the country in March 2000, introducing the broadband concept the same year. DSL broadband over PTCL's copper network followed in 2002.
facts.source: ProPakistani — The Conception and Evolution of Internet

facts.heading: Market Opens Up (2004–2008)
facts.detail: The 2004 Telecom De-regulation Policy allowed private operators to offer FTTH, WiMAX, and cable services. PTCL's cable monopoly ended in 2008 when Transworld Associates brought an alternate international link online.
facts.source: Ispak — About Us; Dawn — Evolution of the Internet in Pakistan

facts.heading: The Fiber Era
facts.detail: Fiber-to-the-home adoption has surged in recent years, growing from under 70,000 subscribers in 2018 to roughly 2.6 million by early 2026.

facts.heading: Infrastructure Is Still Fragile
facts.detail: Pakistan's reliance on a small number of submarine cables and PTCL's dominant share of national bandwidth (around 70%) means single points of failure still cause nationwide disruption — as seen in outages in August 2022, January 2025, and August 2025.
